e1-emuA:
Too often I’ve seen communities focus on the aspect of their project that was most interesting to the original founders, for example political types getting super into writing by-laws, or spiritual types just meditating all the time, or therapists processing each other, or people who like psychedelics discovering they’re all God together and never getting to the point of deciding who will put their name on the deed.

I’ve arbitrarily (at least to me) separated this model into four parts. Yes, I know it’s a little woo woo to think there could be four things that cover jealousy, kids, land, money, God, taking iboga, etc. But if I can just get through this intro, I can point to some resources I’ve written on each of the first three parts that are available for free online (I’m not going to make them sign up for anything or come to a retreat) and then get to the meat of this article which is mostly about the fourth part.
e1-emuB:
One problem I see a lot of communities face is that they end up solving the part of the problem that is of most interest to the founders, while ignoring the others. The political-minded do bylaws. The spiritual-minded do meditation. The therapists do processing. The psychonauts do ‘everyone is God’ and forget to actually sign over the deed.

I’ve broken this down into four parts for the model I propose. It’s an arbitrary number, obviously the details are complicated, and jealousy, kids, money, land, god, and iboga don’t fit neatly into four boxes, but let’s go with it. I’ve written detailed articles on the first three already (available for free here, not a sales pitch for a retreat or anything), but this article will be mostly about the fourth.
e2-emuA:
People have been living together for food, housing, logistics etc. What we’re adding is a practice, an inner work we’re all doing together, and the knowledge this is hard but it will payoff in healing. Plus all the outward parts about working for the escuelita, the federation, being able to help other escuelitas, etc. If we don’t have that, what reason do we have to work together all our lives? How is it different than just sharing a property?

We’re not suppressing anything, we’re processing it all. We’re all authority of our own practice but we have this container. Things are fluid, organic, etc.
e2-emuB:
In a nutshell, it's the difference between working together just to provide food/housing/logistics, etc., and working together to support each other in an internal practice. Why would we want to risk our lives for each other if the only thing we have is the need to take care of property? When we're all trying to help each other heal, to stop living in fear, etc, then it makes sense to bind our lives together. And when we take on the purpose of an outward escuelita and federation, then we have even more reason to do so, because we're not only helping each other build, but others as well.

We don't suppress anything. We process it all. The authority is in the practice. The community is the container. Answers are fluid and organic.
e3-emuA:
These are for the sake of organization, but in reality bleed into each other very often. If I'm writing about jealousy I might put it under governance, because often it comes up when someone is controlling access to a shared resource. Or under medical care if it's about someone lashing out at the healing team. Or under childrearing, or under values, if it's revealing a deep difference in values between the founders. It's mostly so that I can note what I'm not talking about yet.

Whether a community is religious or not, it will have what religious communities would call doctrine. In a secular community it will often be what people call "the process", and it is often just as…
e3-emuB:
These are just rough categories that bleed into one another. In practice, one move in a jealousy situation might also affect how the community governs itself or how it shares resources. Or, the way a community cares for sick members may overlap with status, or the way it raises children may touch on the values of the founders. I mostly break them out like this to help myself see what I am missing when I work with communities, not because living in a community fits neatly into categories.

Some stability in agreements is needed, though. If they are constantly changing, that can be annoying.

In more religious communities, these frozen agreements are called doctrine, but I have seen secular communities make their own kind of doctrine, usually in the form of process.

e5-emuA:
Capacity for assisting the population is not concentrated in a single individual—whether professional, guru, or emotionally necessary founder—but rather diffused among the group.

This means that the people to whom one comes for care do not, as a result of the care relationship, hold authority over one’s other life relationships, such as membership in groups, work, housing, children, medication, or any other kind of “evidence.” If this were the case, the relationship of care would become a relationship of authority, and the supposedly “horizontal” relationship of mutual assistance between peers would once again become vertical.
e5-emuB:
This means that the capacity to help people has to be in the community as a whole, not in a single "professional", "guru", or emotionally essential founder.

It also means that the person helping someone needs to not have any other power over the community - they can't be able to decide whether someone can be a member, or control work, housing, children, medicine, or the "evidence" in a dispute, or anything else. If the person helping someone has power in another role, then it becomes just another step in the hierarchy, and stops being peer care.
e6-emuA:

e7-emuA:
Doing serious plant medicines carefully with peer guidance without exalting any one person as a special shaman.

This doesn't mean it can be done without structure and precautions. People still need to be screened, there should be sober sitters present, emergency plans, integration, boundaries, etc. Yes, it would be pure to have a group of people all get altered and decide the rules together in that state, but I don't recommend it.
e7-emuB:
Participating in serious plant medicines in a careful, peer-guided manner without super-special shamans.

This doesn’t mean there shouldn’t be careful screening, sober sitters, emergency preparedness, attention to integration, etc. It would be very pure to set the rules together while several people are altered at the same time but I wouldn’t recommend it.
e8-emuA:
Membership, Land, Resources, Governance, Children, Leaving

I imagine that in the long run all of these communities will move to a situation with less and less money. I see three stages:

No one buys from anyone else in the community to meet their basic needs, but each person may work outside the community and bring in money. However, if they do work outside, they contribute an agreed upon amount of their income to the community. I imagine this is the only way to realistically get started in the near future.
e8-emuB:
Membership, Land, Resources, Governance, Children, Leaving

I think that eventually, I want to be in a community where there is less and less money involved. Maybe, for now, the best thing to think about is that there will be a stage 1, stage 2 and stage 3.

Stage 1: Nothing is bought from each other to live (food, housing, care, tools, education, transportation, etc). If people have jobs outside of the community, whatever money they make is agreed upon by all to be turned over to the community. (This is probably the best place to start, realistically).
e9-emuA: Of course, as it says later on in the document, any money people make outside of the community (either from wages or from their own businesses) would go towards the common purse and no individual would be able to accumulate wealth while being a member of the community. This is how, for example, the Bruderhof community works (my dad spent 17 years in the Bruderhof). It’s also similar to the way many other income-sharing communities, like Twin Oaks, work.
e9-emuB: Another feature to be implemented at a later date is that all wages and other income earned by the members from work outside the community, or from business inside the community, will be paid into the common purse of the community. No member will be permitted to accumulate private wealth while a member of the community. This is the way things have always been done in the Bruderhof community, in which my father lived for 17 years. It is also done, in a somewhat different way, at Twin Oaks, and a number of other income-sharing communities.
e10-emuA: What I'd like to see eventually is a point where even outside of the community, no money is used. This would not involve barter, but rather a system of goods/gifts/work/obligation/etc. I don't know of any modern community that has gone this far (I'm looking for good sources of information here), and in fact, it may be impossible due to government forces such as taxes on land, etc. Perhaps the end point here is a community that is nearly entirely moneyless, but has a small collective cash boundary on the outside.
e10-emuB: In the furthest goal, the community would also stop using money outside. People would meet their needs directly, or through exchange (be it trade, gift, work, obligation, or whatever) with other people. I don't know of any modern communities that have gotten this far and that I know about well. Various governments make it hard, sometimes literally impossible, to get this far. Various governments impose taxes on land, so there's no way to have a community without at least paying those taxes. So the end of the road would be to have a community that is almost entirely without money, except for a small boundary of cash at the edge.
e11-emuA:
These things can be controlled without money. Access to food and stores, housing, tools, land, medicine, transportation and access to outside currency, if needed. These are all things that need to be thought about in a money free community.

They tend to be a bit less spiritually exciting though. It is hard to have an ecstatic spiritual vision about how to improve the policy on provisional members, or how to calculate a departing member's share of the community's resources, or how to prevent one of the founders of the community from being in control of the land, or what to do when a child reports that
e11-emuB:
This doesn’t even start to cover all the areas where such power can be wielded: access to food storage, housing, tools, land, medicine, transportation, and access to the outside world’s currency, to name a few. Even in a moneyless community there are many ways to create and control scarcity. What are the policies for distribution of these things? What are the expectations for members? What happens when someone wants to leave?

These are less exciting topics to discuss spiritually. It’s rare that someone will come back from an ecstatic vision with news of how to revamp the community’s policies on provisional members, or how to divvy up assets with a departing member, or how to prevent one founder from having control over the land, or how to deal with reports from a child.
e12-emuA:
No amount of beautiful land can make up for a lack of clarity in land ownership. No amount of peer counseling can make up for an overloaded membership process. No amount of medicine can make up for a lack of an exit agreement.

These first three parts create a container for everything else to happen in.

If it is left out, it will end up being addressed later in a pressure-cooker scenario, with the addition of stakes (land, work, resources) and opinions.
e12-emuB:
It’s hard to live on beautiful land if the ownership isn’t clear. It’s hard to do peer counseling if the membership process has admitted too many people. It’s hard to have medicine when there’s no exit agreement.

These first three parts help create the container for everything else.

If they are skipped they will need to be dealt with eventually, usually at high stress, after the group has invested land, labor, and other resources and everyone has an opinion on how things should be.
